title: Digital twin oncology and multi-omics-driven artificial intelligence models for personalized drug response prediction: A systematic survey of emerging computational paradigms and clinical implementation challenges.
text: The increasing complexity of tumor heterogeneity and variable therapeutic response has intensified the need for accurate personalized drug response prediction in oncology. Traditional trial-and-error chemotherapy strategies often result in suboptimal outcomes, toxicity, and delayed therapeutic adjustments. Rapid advances in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin modeling have significantly reshaped computational oncology research. This survey systematically reviews peer-reviewed research and review articles published from 2021 onward that investigate emerging computational paradigms integrating digital twins and multi-omics AI for drug response prediction. The foundational concepts in digital twin oncology, multi-omics profiling and AI-driven precision medicine are outlined initially. The existing approaches are categorized into four major paradigms such as omics-driven machine learning models, deep learning based multimodal architectures, mechanistic digital twin simulation frameworks and hybrid digital twin AI systems enabling adaptive therapy optimization. The multi-omics data integration strategies, including early, intermediate, late, network-based and graph/pathway-based fusion techniques. The survey synthesizes recent developments in drug sensitivity prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, tumor evolution forecasting and virtual clinical trials, while critically analyzing challenges related to data heterogeneity, interpretability, generalization, privacy, regulatory compliance and ethical considerations. Finally, future directions are highlighted such as real-time adaptive digital twins, federated learning, explainable AI and regulatory ready clinical deployment frameworks. Overall, this review provides a structured taxonomy, comparative analysis and research roadmap for advancing integrated digital twin and multi omics AI systems toward clinically actionable precision oncology.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Precision Nutrition: From Multi-Omics Integration to Personalized Dietary Interventions.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a tool for precision nutrition because it can analyse heterogeneous dietary, clinical, physiological, behavioural, and molecular data. This narrative review critically examines how machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, explainable AI, continuous glucose monitoring, wearable technologies, and multi-omics approaches may support individualized nutritional assessment and decision-making. Particular attention is given to the distinction between predictive research, digital personalized nutrition, AI-enabled clinical interventions, and commercial nutrition platforms. Current evidence shows that personalized digital nutrition can improve selected dietary behaviours, while observational AI and multi-omics studies can predict substantial inter-individual variation in metabolic responses. Importantly, evidence that an AI-enabled intervention improves clinical outcomes is still limited and is concentrated in selected settings, including a multicentre randomized trial of an AI-based dietary management platform in adults with type 2 diabetes. Emerging technologies such as large language models, digital twins, federated learning, and adaptive algorithms remain promising but require prospective clinical validation. Major barriers include data quality, algorithmic bias, privacy, interoperability, model transparency, regulatory uncertainty, and limited external validation. Future research should prioritize pragmatic multicentre randomized trials, transparent reporting of model performance, independent validation, health-economic evaluation, and clinically meaningful outcomes. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct to evidence-based nutritional care rather than a replacement for professional clinical judgement. The review differs from technology-centred and methodology-focused reviews by explicitly linking AI modalities and multi-omics data with evidence maturity, clinical trial findings, implementation barriers, and the level of inference justified for each technology.

title: Artificial intelligence in basic and translational cardiovascular research.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in cardiovascular research where conventional analysis struggles with scale, heterogeneity, and multimodal integration. Its contribution differs across imaging, computational omics, mechanistic simulation, and drug discovery. This narrative review examines substantive applications of machine learning and deep learning while distinguishing them from routine bioinformatics and purely biophysical modeling. We assess independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference in representative studies. Deep-learning imaging systems can provide reproducible quantitative phenotypes, but workflow performance alone does not establish mechanism. In single-cell and spatial studies, clustering, integration, trajectory inference, and network reconstruction generally yield associations or hypotheses unless experimentally supported. Mechanistic interpretation is bounded by the specific effect established through targeted perturbation or rescue with functional testing; lineage tracing and orthogonal readouts provide complementary support, not standalone proof of causation. Hybrid AI-biophysical models may accelerate personalized simulation, whereas heart-on-chip, engineered tissue, and organoid systems without learned components are validation platforms rather than AI methods. In drug discovery, active learning and molecular redesign can prioritize candidates, but predicted reductions in ion-channel liability do not demonstrate biological safety or reduced proarrhythmic risk. Major limitations include pseudoreplication, data leakage, domain shift, batch effects, uncertain labels, few independent hearts, demographic imbalance, incomplete calibration, and limited transfer among animal, iPSC-derived, and adult human systems. AI is most valuable when it produces robust phenotypes or experimentally testable hypotheses within a transparent validation framework, rather than when predictive accuracy is treated as mechanistic evidence.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Medicine: A Review from Medical Imaging and Physiological Signals to Genomics, Drug Discovery and Trustworthy Deployment
text: Precision medicine aims to fit diagnosis and treatment to the individual patient, and artificial intelligence has become one of its main tools. Deep networks now read computed tomography scans, mammograms, skin images and echocardiograms; classifiers interpret electrocardiogram and electroencephalogram signals; and learned models predict protein structures and drug–target interactions. The problem is that these advances are reported in separate literatures, each with its own data types, metrics and failure modes, and the barriers to clinical use, such as privacy, bias and security, are usually discussed apart from the models they constrain. This review brings imaging, physiological signals, clinical risk prediction, genomics and drug discovery, and trustworthy deployment into one framework. It organizes 37 studies into a five-layer taxonomy and compares their data, methods and reported results. Imaging studies report expert-level performance, including an area under the curve of 0.944 for lung cancer screening and fewer false positives and false negatives in breast screening, but also show weaker performance on darker skin tones. Signal studies report a deep network that exceeded the average cardiologist in arrhythmia detection, and automated machine learning improved cardiovascular risk prediction over the Framingham score. Genomic and drug discovery studies show that deep models can predict protein structure with near-experimental accuracy and can find new antibiotics. Deployment studies show that federated learning across 20 institutions improved average accuracy by 16% over single-site models, while privacy, security and explainability remain open. Few studies combine more than one data layer, and fairness is rarely measured. Future work should develop multimodal models trained under privacy guarantees and evaluated across diverse patient groups.

title: Converging quality by design, artificial intelligence, and biofoundry automation: A new paradigm for scalable circular biomanufacturing.
text: Synthetic biology applies engineering principles to the rational design of biological systems with the aim of producing predictable and tunable behaviour. Although the field's conceptual foundations and core technologies are well established, the recent simultaneous maturation of Quality by Design (QbD), artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted biological design, and automated biofoundry workflows is beginning to outline a more replicable pathway from laboratory innovation to industrial-scale circular biomanufacturing. This review argues that the convergence of these three elements, rather than any one alone, characterises the current phase of the field. We examine how the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle is being transformed from a research heuristic into a systematic industrial development framework; show how shared toolsets now transfer across microbial, plant, and animal systems to enable a holistic bioeconomy; benchmark synthetic biology-derived products against conventional alternatives where techno-economic and life-cycle data permit; and examine scale-up, regulatory, and societal bottlenecks through recent market-scale case studies in which these bottlenecks have been navigated in practice. We also contrast EU and US regulatory frameworks to show how policy divergence shapes technology adoption. We conclude by identifying what the coming decade of convergent synthetic biology must deliver to support a circular bioeconomy at the scale the 2030 Agenda demands.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping the cancer care continuum—from early detection to personalized treatment—by leveraging capabilities in image recognition, multimodal data integration, and clinical decision support. This paper systematically reviews key AI applications in oncology, including diagnostic imaging, pathology analysis, treatment optimization, and toxicity prediction. It contextualizes these advancements within real-world implementations, such as Andhra Pradesh's newly launched precision oncology ecosystem and the deployment of AI-powered pulmonary nodule screening. The review finds that while AI achieves performance comparable to specialist physicians in specific diagnostic tasks, its clinical value remains constrained by limited external validation, data heterogeneity, and the maturity of human-AI collaboration workflows. We argue that AI's appropriate role in oncology is to augment—not replace—clinical judgment, and that scalable impact depends on coordinated progress in infrastructure integration, regulatory frameworks, and continuous performance monitoring. **1. title: Recent approaches to modulate citrinin biosynthesis in Monascus species: a review.
text: The filamentous fungi Monascus spp. are rich sources of secondary metabolites that include Monascus azaphilone pigments, monacolin K, and γ-aminobutyric acid, making them significant in the food, nutraceutical, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Despite the industrial importance of this fungus, its production of citrinin, a nephrotoxic polyketide mycotoxin, remains a major drawback and limits its commercial application. Recent research studies have shown that the mechanism that governs citrinin biosynthesis highlights the interactions between Biosynthetic Gene Clusters (BGCs), epigenetic modifications, global regulatory networks, and environmental factors. The current understanding of the molecular and epigenetic mechanisms used to mitigate citrinin production in Monascus spp. is discussed in this review. Emphasis is given on histone acetylation and deacetylation, methylation, chromatin remodeling, the velvet complex, and the modulation of toxin biosynthesis through RNA-level gene expression control. The recent advances are critically evaluated for engineering citrinin-free strains, including transcriptomics, proteomics, multi-omics, RNA interference, CRISPR/Cas genome editing, and synthetic biology. The comparative analysis of these approaches shows that integrating epigenetic engineering with advanced genome and metabolic engineering can regulate citrinin while maintaining other important metabolite yields. Combining multi-omics and artificial intelligence-guided strain design with epigenetic interventions will accelerate the development of safe, sustainable, and high-yielding Monascus-assisted bioprocesses. Citrinin biosynthesis in Monascus is shown alongside epigenetic regulation, environmental factors, and control strategies. Histone acetylation activates citrinin genes, while deacetylation represses them; histone methylation can activate or repress biosynthetic gene clusters. DNA and RNA methylation affect transcript stability, translation, development, and metabolite production. Environmental factors include light, carbon and nitrogen sources, pH, and oxidative stress. Control strategies include fermentation optimization, epigenetic modifiers, gene editing, metabolic engineering, citrinin-free strains, and RNA interference targeting pksCT.

title: CRISPR-Cas Systems in Protozoan Parasites: Genome Editing, Functional Genomics, Gene Regulation and Emerging Applications.
text: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

title: CRISPR, mRNA, and Beyond: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Allergy and Immunology.
text: The management of allergic and immunologic diseases has long centered on symptom management rather than disease modification. Conventional pharmacotherapy controls manifestations of the immune dysregulation but does little to treat the underlying cause. Newer monoclonal and small molecule therapies target downstream effectors of the type 2 inflammatory cascade, and allergen immunotherapy, while disease-modifying, requires years of administration for effect. Nucleic acid therapies represent a different approach that intervenes at the level of genetic information itself, at the DNA, RNA, or protein-production step. This includes mRNA treatments that direct cells to produce therapeutic proteins or modify allergen-specific immune responses; antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs that selectively silence disease genes; adeno-associated viral vectors for sustained gene delivery; and CRISPR-based systems that permanently edit the genome. Several technologies have advanced to clinical proof of concept including a CRISPR gene-editing therapy (lonvoguran ziclumeran) that reduced hereditary angioedema attacks by 87% compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial. An inhaled DNAzyme targeting the intracellular transcription factor GATA3 attenuated allergen-induced late asthmatic responses by 34% in humans, and CD19 CAR-T cell therapy induced drug-free remission in severe autoimmune disease. As of 2025, 24 oligonucleotide therapeutics have received FDA approval, including donidalorsen, the first RNA-targeted prophylactic therapy approved for hereditary angioedema. This review examines each therapeutic technology, its mechanism and delivery strategy, and the evidence relevant to allergic and immunologic disease. Persistent challenges, including delivery beyond the liver, immune responses to viral vectors, and the need for long-term safety data, are addressed alongside a proposed integration with existing treatment paradigms.

title: CRISPR Technology: From Bench to Bedside Applications.
text: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
text: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Deciphering the Mechanisms Underlying Therapeutic Resistance in Cancer through Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Technologies: Current Approaches and Future Perspectives.
text: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies are recent high-throughput sequencing advancements that enable transcriptome-wide profiling and characterization of cellular populations at single-cell resolution while preserving tissue spatial context. Their integration has been increasingly applied to cancer research, facilitating a deeper understanding of tumor biology and improving diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Growing evidence suggests that combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with ST offers a robust approach for exploring mechanisms underlying therapeutic resistance. Together, these technologies support the prediction and monitoring of treatment responses and help identify novel therapeutic targets by revealing critical signaling pathways and immune cell populations associated with resistance. Artificial intelligence, including deep learning, computer vision, and generative models, further enhances the integration and analysis of data generated by scRNA-seq and ST, contributing to tumor resistance research. This review summarizes recent advances in the integrated application of scRNA-seq and ST to study tumor resistance and discusses the opportunities, challenges, and future directions of these technologies as a theoretical foundation for identifying therapeutic targets and developing treatment strategies.

title: AI-powered virtual cells, digital twins and agentic AI are reshaping multi-omics, spatial biology and drug discovery.
text: Predicting individual disease trajectories and treatment responses remains challenging in drug discovery. Molecular profiling provides static snapshots that miss cellular dynamics, spatial context and adaptive responses. The convergence of single-cell and spatial omics with generative AI is driving a paradigm shift toward AI-powered virtual cells that model cellular states, interactions and treatment responses. This review introduces a nested framework of six capabilities for AI-powered virtual cells, spanning population-derived models, digital twins and agentic twins. Virtual cells generate synthetic cellular states and predict responses from population data. Digital twins link models to specific biological counterparts, enabling longitudinal updating and prospective prediction. Agentic twins add spatial context, biologically constrained interactions and actions, and environmental feedback, enabling personalized, dynamic and interactive representations of cellular ecosystems. This narrative review is based on literature acquired from PubMed, Web of Science, bioRxiv and arXiv searches up to October 2026. AI-powered virtual cells could support drug discovery as foundation models that transfer biological knowledge across tasks, including data-limited settings. Their value depends on faithful extrapolation beyond training data and prospective validation against biological observations. Coupling these models to repeatedly measured experimental systems could enable personalized prediction, iterative updating and prioritization of perturbations, targets and therapeutic strategies.

title: Dynamic changes in mRNA isoform usage during human retinal organoid development
text: Alternative mRNA splicing is a key mechanism for generating isoform diversity in eukaryotic cells. However, the extent of the splicing changes that occur during complex regulatory processes like neurodevelopment are still incompletely characterized. We perform nanopore-based long-read RNA sequencing on differentiating human stem cell-derived retinal organoids to identify temporal patterns of isoform usage across developmental stages. We find that retinal organoids undergo dynamic shifts in isoform usage throughout differentiation, which are not necessarily accompanied with changes in overall gene expression, as is observed for many genes involved in the regulation of mRNA splicing itself. Further analysis of human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells uncovers neuron-specific splicing signatures. Additionally, allele-specific gene expression analysis reveals extensive allelic imbalance in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived organoid cultures. By combining direct long-read RNA sequencing with human stem cell retinal models we develop a comprehensive database of isoform-level changes in differentiating human retinal organoid cells during development. These results uncover dynamic shifts in transcript usage during retinal differentiation, adding to our knowledge base of post-transcriptional RNA processing in the developing central nervous system and human in vitro culture systems.

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges.
text: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

title: Longevitomics as the Science of the Longevitome: Towards a Unified Systems Science of Healthy Longevity.
text: The twenty-first century has transformed longevity research through genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, microbiome science, digital phenotyping and artificial intelligence. Yet healthy longevity remains difficult to explain because its determinants are commonly studied as separate molecular layers, mechanisms or biomarkers. Here, we introduce Longevitomics as an integrative systems framework for understanding, modeling and predicting healthy longevity and define the Longevitome inspired by the Latin expression vita longa (long life) as the dynamic architecture of biological, environmental and behavioral determinants that collectively shape psychosomatic resilience across the life course. We position this proposal in relation to the Hallmarks of Aging, geroscience, biological-age biomarkers, multi-omics and systems medicine. Longevitomics is not intended to replace these established frameworks or to constitute another molecular "ome." Rather, it provides a systems-level framework in which mechanistic hallmarks, multi-omic layers, physiological phenotypes, exposures and adaptive responses can be integrated longitudinally. We further consider how network analysis, causal inference, machine learning and digital-twin approaches may enable reconstruction of individual Longevitome trajectories and support a transition toward predictive and personalized longevity medicine.

title: The road ahead for stem cell therapies in type 1 diabetes.
text: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells. Although exogenous insulin remains the standard treatment, it does not restore physiological glucose regulation. Differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells into β-cells offers a scalable alternative to cadaveric islet transplantation and has progressed rapidly over the past decade, resulting in nine clinical trials at various stages of completion. Despite this progress, durable graft function remains constrained by two major challenges: the absence of key islet microenvironment components, such as vasculature, extracellular matrix and supporting cell types and continued vulnerability to autoimmune and alloimmune rejection. This review considers emerging technological approaches to overcome these barriers. Bioengineered niches, including multilineage organoids, functionalized hydrogels, decellularized matrices and bioprinting, aim to recreate the native islet microenvironment, while synthetic biology approaches, such as hypoimmune gene editing, CRISPR-based transcriptional control and stimulus-responsive survival circuits, seek to enhance grafts' resilience. Computational and single-cell approaches, including gene regulatory network analysis and digital twin frameworks, are beginning to provide predictive tools for benchmarking differentiation quality and forecasting graft outcomes. Together, these complementary strategies, potentially tailored to individual patients, represent a realistic path towards safer, more effective and durable β-cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes.

title: Theranostic Imaging Agents: Integrating Molecular Diagnostics, Precision Therapeutics, and Artificial Intelligence.
text: Theranostic imaging agents combine molecular diagnosis, targeted therapy and monitoring of treatment response into a single paradigm of precision medicine. This review summarizes the current development and translational landscape of theranostic imaging agents, covering molecular targets, imaging platforms, principles of agent design, nanotheranostics, radiotheranostics, and disease-specific applications. Particular emphasis is given to clinically validated and emerging targeting strategies using prostate-specific membrane antigen, somatostatin receptors, fibroblast activation protein, C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) and other disease-associated biomarkers. Moreover, the review addresses Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), optical, photoacoustic, Raman and multimodal imaging approaches, therapeutic payloads, stimulus-responsive systems, and pharmacokinetic optimization. Moreover, emerging applications of artificial intelligence, radiomics, radiogenomics, spatial and single-cell multiomics, liquid biopsy, digital pathology, personalized dosimetry, and digital twins are evaluated for their potential to improve patient stratification, treatment selection, response assessment and adaptive therapy. Despite tremendous progress, clinical translation is hampered by target heterogeneity, off-target accumulation, radionuclide availability, manufacturing complexity, dosimetric uncertainty, regulatory requirements, limited clinical validation, data interoperability, cost and unequal access. This review, overall, emphasizes the convergence of molecular imaging, targeted therapeutics, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence in the development of next-generation theranostic platforms, and outlines critical priorities for their clinical translation.

title: Digital twin technology in cardiovascular care: future perspectives for nursing practice, patient management, and clinical decision-making.
text: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of mortality globally and continue to impose substantial clinical, economic, and organisational burdens on healthcare systems due to increasing disease complexity, recurrent hospitalisations, and the need for long-term monitoring and personalised care. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, computational modelling, wearable biosensors, telehealth, and digital health technologies have accelerated the emergence of Digital Twin Technology (DTT) as a promising innovation in precision cardiovascular healthcare. Although DTT has gained growing attention in medicine and engineering, its implications for cardiovascular nursing practice, patient management, and clinical decision-making remain insufficiently synthesised. This scoping review aimed to explore the current applications of DTT in cardiovascular healthcare and examine its implications for cardiovascular nursing practice, patient management, clinical decision-making, and future healthcare delivery. Review was conducted using the Arksey and O'Malley methodological framework and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar was performed for studies published between 2020 and 2026. Eligible studies included literature related to digital twins, computational cardiovascular modelling, artificial intelligence-assisted cardiovascular care, wearable technologies, remote monitoring systems, and nursing implications in cardiovascular healthcare. Data were charted and synthesised narratively according to predefined research questions and thematic areas. Thirty studies met the inclusion criteria. The findings demonstrated that DTT is increasingly applied in heart failure monitoring, arrhythmia prediction, telecardiology, smart ICU systems, virtual cardiac modelling, personalised rehabilitation, and population-level cardiovascular risk prediction. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, wearable biosensors, cloud computing, electronic health records, and predictive analytics were the most commonly reported technological components. The review further identified important implications for cardiovascular nursing, including transition from reactive to predictive care, expansion of telehealth nursing, enhanced data-driven clinical decision-making, and the growing need for digital competency. However, ethical concerns, cybersecurity risks, interoperability challenges,infrastructure costs, workforce preparedness, and limited nursing-focused evidence remain significant barriers. DTT has the potential to transform cardiovascular healthcare through predictive, personalised, and continuously adaptive models of care. Strengthening nursing leadership, digital competency and interdisciplinary collaboration is essential for integration of DTT into future cardiovascular practice.

title: A Non-interventional, International, Multicentre Clinical Research Study to Build the Largest Collection of Multimodal Data (Including Clinical Data, Imaging Data and Omics Data) in Oncology
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] Cancer is amongst the leading causes of disease-related morbidity and mortality. A major challenge in cancer treatment is the development of biology-informed, personalised treatment strategies. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have shed further insights into disease biology and treatment pathways, thus identifying new, precision medicine-based therapeutic opportunities. The biological mechanisms leading to cancer development and progression arise from complex and plastic networks of dysregulated cellular programs involving many signalling pathways and effector molecules. Cancer cells alter their surrounding environment via cell-cell interactions with non-tumor cells or by secreting cytokines, chemokines and other factors. This reprogramming of the tumour microenvironment (TME) is critical for cancer progression, invasion, and metastasis. Moreover, there are increasing studies that show that both innate and adaptive immune cell types contribute to tumorigenesis and treatment resistance when present within the TME. Understanding the crosstalk between cancer cells and the surrounding TME will inform on mechanisms of sensitivity and resistance to treatment, including immunotherapy (IO) and targeted therapies. Spatially resolved-Omics is an emerging field that characterises cell types by gene/protein expressions within their spatial context in the tissue organisation. Recent high profile spatial transcriptomics studies have uncovered specific cell identities that define the surrounding TME. The MOSAIC study, a collaborative initiative across industry and top oncology hospitals, proposes to go way beyond current cancer molecular profiling projects by combining the generation and analysis of multiple data modalities (3 essential mandatory modalities: Clinical Data, Hematoxylin and Eosin (H\&E) microscopic image, Spatial transcriptomics; up to 3 high priority data modalities depending on technical feasibility and sample size: bulk Ribonucleic Acid Sequencing (RNAseq), bulk Whole Exome Sequencing (WES), Single-cell transcriptomics; and potentially other optional data modalities and follow-up experiments such as single-cell omics, immunohistochemistry and spatial proteomics or other molecular profiling of proteins and molecules) on a minimum of 2,000 tumour samples across a different cancer indications. This will generate broad molecular and cellular profiling data of the tumour and its microenvironment from cancer patients, integrated with clinical data, at an unprecedented scale and resolution. This study will enroll patients diagnosed with one of the eligible cancer indications and for which a formalin fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tumor sample from already performed biopsy and/or surgical resection is available within their local pathology archive or their affiliate centers archives. The MOSAIC study expects to have a strong impact for patients in terms of new targeted therapeutic drug discovery, identification of patient subgroups requiring either specific treatment or broader clinical care and identification of novel treatment response and resistance mechanisms.

title: GenoMed4ALL: Improving SCD Classification and Prognosis by AI
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: UNKNOWN] GenoMed4All 'Genomics and Personalized Medicine for all though Artificial Intelligence in Haematological Diseases' aims to advance on individual SCD patients' disease characterisation and to improve the monitoring of patients' health status, optimise clinical therapy guidance and ultimately improved health outcomes by the identification of biomarkers and the development of individual (risk) models in SCD. Genomed4All supports the pooling of genomic, clinical data and other "-omics" health through a secure and privacy respectful data sharing platform based on the novel Federated Learning scheme, to advance research in personalised medicine in haematological diseases thanks to advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) models and standardised interoperable sharing of cross-border data, without needing to directly share any sensitive clinical patients' data. The SCD Use case will gather multi-modal clinical and -OMICs data from 1,000 SCD patients in 4 EU-MS: France, Italy, Spain and The Netherlands. In close collaboration with the European Reference Network on Rare Hematological Diseases (ERN-EuroBloodNet, GA101157011), GENOMED4ALL involves multiple clinical partners from the network, while leveraging on healthcare information and repositories that will be gathered incorporating interoperability standards as promoted by ERN-EuroBloodNet central registry, the European Rare Blood Disorders Platform.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven pharmacovigilance: transforming signal detection, real-world drug safety monitoring, and regulatory decision-making.
text: Pharmacovigilance is undergoing rapid transformation due to the expansion of digital healthcare systems, biomedical data generation, and pharmaceutical innovation. Conventional drug-safety monitoring methods remain limited by underreporting, delayed signal identification, fragmented datasets, and restricted predictive capability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for improving signal detection, real-world drug-safety surveillance, and regulatory decision-making. This review evaluates application of AI technologies in modern pharmacovigilance and regulatory science. It discusses use of machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, and natural language processing for adverse-event detection, literature mining, signal prioritization, and analysis of electronic health records (EHR) and social-media data. Emerging technologies, including large language models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring systems, are also explored. Literature was identified through structured searches of MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering publications from January 2000 to February 2026. AI-driven pharmacovigilance has potential to improve real-time safety surveillance, predictive risk assessment, and automated regulatory workflows. However, broader implementation remains challenged by concerns related to interpretability, data quality, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and regulatory validation. Future progress will depend on transparent, explainable, and human-supervised AI systems integrated within globally interoperable healthcare infrastructures.

title: Multi-omics signatures indicative of status and effectiveness of vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 in ferrets
text: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted one of the most rapid vaccination efforts in history in an attempt to mitigate the global health and socio-economic burden of the disease. Today, the challenge remains in maintaining vaccine efficacy given the continuous evolution of key antigenic sites in the viral Spike protein. Access to multi-omics data analysis and machine learning (ML) approaches has greatly enhanced our ability to evaluate biomarkers associated with diagnosis, prognosis, drug discovery, and therapeutics, and can be used to obtain additional insights from traditional efficacy studies. In this study, multi-omics data (transcriptomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics) were processed from 16 ferrets vaccinated with DNA vaccines based on Wuhan-Hu-1 and SynCon spike sequences. Multi-omics data was integrated into Random Forest models to identify potential biomarkers indicative of vaccination status and the development of neutralising antibody titres against six SARS-CoV-2 variants. Causal analysis, based on Empirical Bayes Matrix Factorisation, was used to identify biological processes occurring between vaccination and a positive immune response. Several putative transcriptomic, lipid and metabolite biomarkers associated with reducing hyper-inflammation and maintaining cell homeostasis were identified using Random Forest models incorporating the omics analyses. These were similarly found when using vaccine immune response as class labels. Additionally, causal analysis identified four and three latent factors associated with vaccination status and response, respectively. Within these, several enriched gene sets relating to cell function and regulation, including ATP-synthesis and mitochondrial related processes were identified. Other genes also included those with secondary immune functions, particularly relating to chemokine and cytokines. This study provides a holistic analysis of ferret immune response to SARS-CoV-2 by integrating multi-omics data with ML and casual analysis and potential targets for further investigation.

title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.
text: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

title: Application of Machine Learning Algorithms to Health Systems Planning and Public Policy Using Real-World Data: Scoping Review.
text: The rapid advancement of information technology and machine learning (ML) has garnered significant interest from health care managers and policymakers. However, incorporating reliable and transparent predictions into health systems remains challenging, necessitating an investigation into gaps in digital health interventions within real-world settings characterized by resource constraints and reliability issues. This study aimed to map and synthesize the available evidence on the application of ML algorithms to real-world data in health systems and identify their operational targets and clinical implications for health planning and public policy formulation. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines, we searched the PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and LILACS databases for empirical studies published between 2016 and 2025 that evaluated the application of ML to health management, surgical queues, and public policy using real-world data. The study protocol was retrospectively registered with the OSF. Of the studies identified through the database searches (2016-2025), only 6 empirical studies met all inclusion criteria, revealing that the real-world deployment of ML in health management and public policy remains at an early stage. The included models addressed micro-operational tasks, such as surgical blood transfusion forecasting, early warning system mortality prediction, postsurgical discharge planning, laboratory error detection, patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) prediction, and emergency care classification. Although high discriminatory performance was reported (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.76-0.99), the studies were limited by single-center retrospective designs, a lack of independent external validation, and inadequate reporting of model calibration. Current evidence on ML for macrolevel health planning and public policy formulation is limited and micro-operationally focused. Translating these algorithms into public health governance (eg, waiting list regulation in universal health systems such as the Sistema Único de Saúde [SUS]) requires moving beyond "black-box" predictions toward explainable AI (XAI), natural language processing (NLP) to analyze unstructured data, transparent model calibration, and rigorous evaluations of health equity.

title: Multi-omics profiling identifies a CXCL9-PD-1+ CD8+ T cell axis for prediction of checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis.
text: Checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP) is a life-threatening complication of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). We aimed to identify predictive biomarkers associated with symptomatic CIP (sCIP) and unravel the underlying pathogenesis. We integrated CyTOF, proteomics, single-cell RNA and V(D)J sequencing, single-cell secretomics, and spatial transcriptomics. These techniques were used to profile peripheral blood, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and lung tissue samples from two prospective multi-center cohorts of NSCLC patients receiving ICI combination treatments. Elevated serum CXCL9 levels combined with high frequencies of peripheral PD-1+ CD8+ T cells after induction ICI were associated with subsequent sCIP (AUC=0.954) and inferior overall survival (HR=7.19, p=0.004). Mechanistically, PD-1+ CD8+ T cells displayed a type 1 effector profile characterized by IFN-γ and MIP-1β secretion. CXCL9/CXCR3 signaling was associated with recruitment of these cells to inflamed lung tissue. The CXCL9-PD-1+ CD8+ T cell axis is associated with CIP pathogenesis. This mechanism supports a potential blood-based biomarker model for CIP risk stratification and identifies a promising preventive therapeutic target to optimize clinical management.

title: AI-driven multi-omics identifies SPP1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages as a therapeutic target and predicts lymph node metastasis in papillary thyroid cancer.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming drug design by enabling the systematic discovery of therapeutic targets and the prediction of drug response from complex biomedical data. In papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), lymph node metastasis remains a key determinant of poor outcome, yet targetable drivers and predictive models for metastasis are lacking. Here, we integrate single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and machine learning to identify SPP1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as a functionally validated driver of lymph node metastasis in PTC. Using single-cell and spatial analyses, we show that SPP1⁺ TAMs engage TM4SF1⁺ malignant epithelial cells via the SPP1-CD44 axis within a hypoxic niche, driving tumor stemness, invasion, and metastatic progression. SPP1⁺ TAMs exhibit a hypoxic, M2-polarized phenotype and their abundance correlates with worse overall and progression‑free survival in metastatic PTC patients. We further develop an integrative machine-learning model based on SPP1⁺ TAM‑derived molecular features that predicts lymph node status with high accuracy. Preclinically, pharmacological targeting of SPP1 attenuates tumor cell migration, invasion, and lung metastasis, supporting its candidacy as a therapeutic target. Collectively, this study demonstrates how AI‑driven multi‑omics analysis can jointly identify a functionally validated target and generate a clinically deployable predictive model, illustrating a framework for bridging computational discovery with translational oncology.

title: Gene Therapy: Advances in Delivery Systems, Genome Editing Technologies, and Applications in Human and Veterinary Medicine.
text: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.

title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud.
text: To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out-of-the-box, AI-based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. The framework comprises two main components: the Python-native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute-funded resource that supports cloud-hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute-hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open-source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user-friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI-based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose-volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal-tissue complication and tumor-control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr-radiological-radiotherapy-imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ-at-risk (OAR) and lung-nodule segmentation based on published models trained in-house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr-notebooks. The framework facilitates end-to-end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

title: Building Capacity for the Engineering of Biology and Biomanufacturing in Finland.
text: Finland's efforts on engineering biology (synthetic biology) originate from the investments in genetic engineering at the beginning of 1980s. The efforts were linked early on with industry, such as dairy companies, vaccine production and production of ethanol and industrial enzymes, and development of commercial scale bioprocesses. Timely support for activities in metabolic engineering, systems biology and genome wide technologies (omics) and incorporating bioinformatics and cell level modelling evolved the field naturally towards synthetic biology and biofoundry activities. This foundation has created a strong basis in industrial biotechnology in particular, its insights and capabilities being increasingly relevant today within the green transition and bioeconomy contexts. In Finland, more than 830 companies are categorised to operate in biotechnology, collectively producing a turnover of 7.1 billion euros and providing jobs for around 19,400 people. Technology and business opportunities are developing fastest in the field of modern biotechnology rooted in molecular biology. Consequently, in the past 15 years, Finland has evidenced the founding of many new biotechnology firms. In relation to bioeconomy, Finland has also a significant research tradition in plant biotechnology and breeding and in pilot scale cultivation of plant cells. Furthermore, engineering biology activities within medical biotechnology and diagnostics are strong. According to a recent report, 88.5% of the revenue of Finnish biotechnology companies comes from activities classified as industrial biotechnology. This article focuses on engineering/synthetic biology developments for industrial biotechnology, including microbial production of food components and pharma products.

title: From Static Records to Virtual Digital Patients: An Artificial Intelligence-Driven Framework for Medical Data Assetization and Governance.
text: Healthcare data remain difficult to use because of fragmentation, sensitivity, and overlapping rights and responsibilities. A virtual digital patient links a longitudinal representation of an individual patient with modeling capabilities for specified clinical or research questions. This article proposes a conceptual socio-technical framework for governing how virtual digital patients are created, accessed, used, and updated. A narrative synthesis of selected policy, modeling, interoperability, and health artificial intelligence literature informs four interdependent layers: data and representation; artificial intelligence modeling and simulation; governance and control; and clinical and external use. The framework connects standardized longitudinal representations, knowledge-supported reasoning, disease-specific simulation, authorization, output review, lifecycle management, and accountability. It distinguishes data resources, model services, operational capabilities, and potentially recognizable assets; technical functionality alone does not establish asset status. An illustrative oncology trial-design scenario shows how purpose-limited requests could produce bounded, reviewed outputs without transferring raw patient records. A staged validation agenda addresses data quality, model performance, workflow safety, clinical utility, and governance controls. The article reports neither a new algorithm nor a deployed or clinically validated system. Its contribution is an integrated reference architecture for evaluating how patient-specific modeling, institutional stewardship, and value return may be aligned. Disease-specific implementation and empirical evaluation are required before clinical or commercial claims can be established.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care.
text: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, affecting half of the world's population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end "perception-reasoning-intervention" system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
text: Abstract Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases. Single cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTLs) have revealed genetic regulation that drives sub-tissue cell states and types across diverse human tissues. Here, we describe the first phase of TenK10K, the largest-to-date dataset of matched whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). We leverage scRNA-seq data from over 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, and matched WGS, from 1,925 individuals, which provides power to detect associations between rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterised in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell type-specific manner using a recently introduced method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than relying on aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare variant signals for 47% of genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell type and state spectra, develop a framework to determine the degree to which sc-eQTLs are cell type-specific, and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we also further characterise the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states and functions, and effects that vary cell state abundance directly.

title: Current applications of artificial intelligence for advancing agriculture, sustainability and climate mitigation
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Telemedicine: Transforming Diagnosis and Personalized Care in Virtual Health Systems
text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within telemedicine has revolutionized virtual healthcare delivery by enabling high-precision diagnostics and tailored treatment strategies remotely. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art AI models applied to medical imaging and clinical text data within telehealth platforms, highlighting significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support. Using deep learning architectures like ResNet-50 for imaging and BERT for natural language processing of electronic health records, the framework demonstrates enhanced patient care personalization and operational efficiency. Survey feedback from clinicians and patients underscores AI's practical benefits in improving healthcare accessibility and quality in remote settings. Challenges, including algorithmic biases and data privacy risks, are discussed, along with future research directions aimed at sustaining AI-driven telemedicine enhancements to health systems worldwide.

title: Yeast-Based Platforms for Next-Generation Human Health Applications
text: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Telemedicine: Transforming Diagnosis and Personalized Care in Virtual Health Systems
text: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within telemedicine has revolutionized virtual healthcare delivery by enabling high-precision diagnostics and tailored treatment strategies remotely. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art AI models applied to medical imaging and clinical text data within telehealth platforms, highlighting significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support. Using deep learning architectures like ResNet-50 for imaging and BERT for natural language processing of electronic health records, the framework demonstrates enhanced patient care personalization and operational efficiency.
