title: Myeloid subpopulations correlate with responsiveness to therapy in a prospective, longitudinal study on RA patients
text: BackgroundRheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease associated with the destruction of cartilage and bone, increased risk of cardiovascular disease and a higher mortality rate. Despite the many therapies that exist for RA, there is little information to guide selection of the most effective treatment for an individual patient. Ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies have created an opportunity to investigate the target tissue. While a number of studies have characterized the stromal and immune cell populations using single-cell technology on synovial biopsy samples, here we performed a longitudinal study, where we collected comprehensive clinical data over a one-year period on each patient in the process of changing their therapy. MethodsSamples from minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were collected from RA patients at baseline prior to start of a new therapy and 4-6-week follow-up under IRB-approved protocols with informed consent. Comprehensive clinical data from each appointment were recorded into a shared REDCap database. Failure to respond to therapy was based on clinical disease activity index (CDAI) for RA after 12-18 weeks post therapy. Biopsied samples were dissociated, enriched for CD45 or CD45CD11b cells, and processed on the 10X Genomics Chromium platform to generate libraries for single-cell RNA sequencing with cell-surface protein detection (CITE-seq). Spatial transcriptomics were performed on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded sections analyzed with 10X Xenium and NanoString CosMx. ResultsWe performed CITE-seq analysis on [~]38,000 CD45+ synovial cells isolated from 17 patients who failed a conventional or biologic DMARD and planned to change therapy. We then subclustered on the myeloid population to reveal 12 myeloid subpopulations that consist of macrophages (n = 8), Osteoclast-like cells, DCs (n = 2) and proliferating cells. The proportion of cDCs was significantly higher in responders, while the proportion of macrophages was significantly lower in responders. The proportion of ISG15+and THBS1+macrophages were enriched in the non-responder patients. Spatial transcriptomics revealed that ISG15+ macrophages were preferentially localized to the synovial lining, while the THBS1+ macrophages are likely interacting with lymphoid cells within the sublining tissue. ConclusionsThese data are among the first to prospectively profile macrophage populations as predictors of response to therapy. Future studies are required to verify whether myeloid subpopulation associations hold across specific therapies.

title: Understanding the control of perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry
text: Consumer demand for year-round strawberry fruit has increased the need to extend the cropping season. Perpetual flowering cultivars, which produce fruit continuously throughout the growing season, offer a promising solution. However, these cultivars typically exhibit reduced runner production, due to a genetic trade-off between flowering and runnering, presenting challenges for propagation and breeding efforts. Additionally, limited understanding of the mechanisms controlling these traits in the cultivated strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) has hindered the application of advanced breeding or crop improvement tools. This PhD work aimed to better understand the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying perpetual flowering and continuous runnering in strawberry, to contribute to the development of perpetual flowering cultivars with extended fruiting periods and improved propagation potential. In this thesis the control of perpetual flowering was explored by functionally studying key f lowering genes TFL1 and FT1 in F. x ananassa seasonal flowering cultivar ‘Malling Centenary’ and perpetual flowering cultivar ‘Calypso’ using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and phenotyping. FaTFL1 mutant lines exhibited early flowering and reduced runner production under long day conditions, validating its role as a floral repressor and demonstrating the regulatory link between these traits. FaFT1 mutant lines presented alteration in floral and fruit morphology suggesting its role in floral development. Furthermore, the genetic regulation of the trade-off between flowering and runnering was studied through genotyping-by-sequencing based QTL mapping using a woodland strawberry (Fragaria vesca) F₂ mapping population developed from a cross between an ecotype from Spain with continuous runnering habit and an accession from Iceland with a “standard” runnering habit. Two additive QTLs associated with continuous runnering were identified using interval mapping. The most significant QTL was narrowed and validated using cleave amplified polymorphic sequences (CAPS) for genotyping in a second validation population. Candidate genes associated with dormancy and axillary bud outgrowth were identified in both QTLs. Gene expression analysis showed a significant downregulation of two candidate genes in continuous runnering individuals supporting their role in the control of this trait. Finally, the functional role of the two main candidate genes for continuous runnering was explored through CRISPR/Cas9 targeted mutagenesis in F. vesca. Two mutant lines for one of the main candidate genes were obtained, however the editing efficiency was very low and consequently this part of the study was not pursued to completion. The work developed within this thesis provides valuable insight into the mechanisms controlling perpetual flowering and the developmental trade-off between generative and vegetative reproduction that could inform future crop improvement strategies.

title: Het opbouwen van ruimtelijke en single-cell transcriptomische atlassen om astrocytenheterogeniteit en -functie in gezondheid en ziekte te ontrafelen
text: Astrocytes comprise one of the major classes of glial cells in the mammalian brain and are essential for central nervous system (CNS) development and function. These cells contribute to diverse processes, including synapse formation, maintenance of synaptic homeostasis through the control of extracellular K+ levels and neurotransmitter clearance, modulation of synaptic transmission, formation and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier, control of cerebral blood flow, and immune responses. Yet,compared with their neuronal counterparts, their diversity and functional specialization remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence supports the existence of a high degree of astrocyte heterogeneity throughout the CNS, both across and within brain regions, during development, and in injury and disease contexts. Importantly, recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) now enable the exploration of astrocyte heterogeneity with unprecedented depth and resolution. Using state-of-the-art single-cell and ST approaches, the overall aim of this project is to uncover different aspects of astrocyte diversity, from molecular heterogeneity in the healthy mouse brain across development and adulthood to heterogenous astrocyte responses in disease. Recent single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies have profiled millions of cells across the mouse brain. However, substantial technical differences between these methods have resulted in the identification of varying numbers of astrocyte populations and the use of distinct nomenclatures, making the alignment of findings across studies challenging. To address this, I established a unified atlas of adult mouse astrocytes by harmonizing multiple single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing datasets into a unified reference framework. This work identified seven major populations and 37 subpopulations that vary in abundance across distinct brain regions and are characterized by specific molecular gene signatures. These findings provide a foundation for the future development of tools to target defined astrocyte populations and manipulate their function. This project further demonstrates how ST can be used to characterize the expression of particularly challenging transcripts, such as clustered protocadherins (cPcdh), which share highly similar sequences. Using a highly sensitive ST approach with subcellular resolution, I generated an atlas of postnatal mouse visual cortical development that enabled the detection of distinct cPcdh transcripts. Particularly, I show that α-cPcdhs are mainly enriched in neurons, whereas γ-cPcdhs are enriched in both neurons and astrocytes, with population-specific enrichment across astrocyte subpopulations. These findings support the idea that different populations of astrocytes may not equally participate in synapse formation and function, with potential implications for neurodevelopmental conditions such as Trisomy 21. Finally, this project extends the study of astrocyte molecular heterogeneity to human disease by generating single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic atlases of the substantia nigra pars compacta from donors with Parkinson's disease (PD) and control donors. Neurodegenerative conditions such as PD have traditionally been considered primary neuronal disorders. However, the contribution of non-neuronal populations in disease pathogenesis and progression remains poorly understood and is increasingly being recognized. Using single-nucleus and ST, I assessed cell-type-specific dysfunction in PD and found that PD is a multicellular disorder. These results support the view that glial cells, including astrocytes, adopt heterogenous molecular states that likely reflect different degrees of vulnerability or resilience in relation to the surrounding diseased environment. Taken together, the work presented in this project provides a multi-scale, spatially resolved view of astrocyte biology, establishing new frameworks to interpret astrocyt

title: Dry eye disease beyond tear deficiency: inflammation, biomarkers, genetics and precision medicine
text: Dry eye disease (DED) is a prevalent multifactorial ocular surface disorder that is associated with instability of the tear film, hyperosmolarity, inflammation, and abnormality of the neurosensory epithelium. Previously thought of as a passive outcome of poor tear production, DED is now recognized as a complex and heterogenous disease involving multiple interacting pathophysiological mechanisms. Inflammation plays an important role in DED, with significant implications on visual performance and quality of life across the globe. Recent advances have improved our understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of DED. Tear hyperosmolarity triggers innate and adaptive immune responses that consist of proinflammatory cytokine release, activation of matrix metalloproteinases, inflammasome, and involvement of the ICAM-1/LFA-1 signaling pathway. These mechanisms lead to chronic inflammation and progression of disease of the ocular surface. Simultaneously, biomarker studies have identified tear cytokines, inflammatory mediators, and multi-marker panels as potential tools for disease diagnosis, patient stratification and treatment monitoring, although their clinical utility requires further validation. Recent studies on systems biology and multi-omics have highlighted the intricate interactions between genetic, molecular, and environmental factors, providing further insight into disease heterogeneity. The growing focus on mechanism-based treatment methods is aided by developments in targeted therapies, such as immunomodulators and new drug delivery systems. The future of DED management will potentially be based on the analysis of biomarkers, genomic data, and clinical phenotypes to support precision medicine. However, further clinical validation is needed to establish whether these approaches can improve individualized diagnosis, treatment selection, and long-term patient outcomes.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA delivery system for cancer management
text: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics have transformed cancer treatment strategies, especially after the success of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled mRNA vaccines. LNPs are effective non-viral delivery vehicles that protect mRNA, enhance intracellular delivery, and improve therapeutic safety. This review discusses recent advancements in LNP-mediated mRNA therapies, including mRNA vaccines, cytokine delivery, immune modulation, and CAR-based strategies. Innovations in lipid formulations and high-throughput technologies have enhanced delivery efficiency. We also discussed how LNP-mRNA formulations elicit immune responses and improve tumor microenvironments. We highlight promising personalized mRNA vaccines and therapies. However, challenges such as tissue specificity, immunogenicity, and manufacturing remain. Emerging strategies in lipid engineering and personalized medicine aim to address these issues, making LNP-mediated mRNA therapeutics a pivotal approach in precision oncology. This report provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in LNP-mRNA therapeutics for cancer treatment. This report also highlights recent innovations and clinical trials. We further highlight the limitations and challenges associated with LNP-mRNA therapeutics in clinical translation. Finally, we outlined the prospects of LNP-based mRNA therapeutics for personalized cancer treatment.

title: Low‐Intensity Focused Ultrasound Enables Temporal Modulation of Human Midbrain Organoid Differentiation
text: ABSTRACT Controlling the precise timing of biosignaling cues in complex 3D models such as organoids is critical for guiding cellular differentiation and functional maturation. Ultrasound stimulation, a next‐generation neuromodulation modality, offers unique advantages due to its target specificity, ability to elicit mechanosensitive responses, and high spatial resolution. However, there is still a lack of precision stimulation platforms and comprehensive biomarker assays for selective control of organoid development. Here, we introduce a modular piezoelectric ultrasound stimulation platform that integrates seamlessly with conventional multi‐well plates, enabling selective neuromodulation of midbrain organoids (mBOs). We demonstrate that ultrasound can specifically modulate cellular differentiation by promoting dopaminergic progenitor markers while delaying terminal differentiation. Importantly, ultrasound stimulation did not induce cellular damage, as confirmed by the absence of apoptosis and DNA damage markers. This work demonstrates the potential of focused ultrasound as a safe, non‐invasive, and tunable biophysical cue for temporal regulation of organoid differentiation.

title: DNA uptake and twitching motility are controlled by small RNA Arp through repression of pilin translation in Acinetobacter baumannii
text: Acinetobacter baumannii is a major opportunistic pathogen capable of natural transformation. This process is driven by type IV pili (T4P) facilitating horizontal gene transfer and accelerating the spread of antimicrobial resistance. While the transcriptional regulation of T4P is increasingly understood, post-transcriptional mechanisms controlling pilus assembly remain unexplored. Here, we identify and mechanistically characterise a small RNA, Arp ( Acinetobacter repressor of pilin), as a post-transcriptional repressor of T4P-mediated functions in A. baumannii . Previous proximity RNA-RNA ligation experiments using High throughput Global sRNA target Identification by Ligation and Sequencing (Hi-GRIL-seq), indicated interactions between Arp and the 5′ end of the pilA mRNA, encoding the major pilin subunit PilA. Here, in-line probing and translational reporter assays revealed that Arp represses pilA translation in A. baumannii by sequestering the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and the first seven codons of the pilA mRNA. Accordingly, deletion of arp increases DNA uptake and twitching motility, while overexpression of Arp depletes pilA mRNA from A. baumannii cells significantly impairing DNA uptake and twitching motility—two hallmark T4P-dependent phenotypes. Together, our study identifies a native A. baumannii sRNA that modulates natural competence by targeting pilin synthesis, revealing a new regulatory layer that could be exploited to disrupt horizontal gene transfer in multidrug-resistant strains.

title: StrataChip: a microphysiological system to capture dynamic keratinocyte fate and mechanical transitions during human epidermal morphogenesis
text: Epidermal development and homeostasis require precise coordination between keratinocyte differentiation and mechanics. Still, the mechanisms integrating these processes remain poorly understood in part due to limitations of existing experimental systems. Here, we introduce StrataChip, a tractable microphysiological system that enables dynamic, multimodal interrogation of human epidermal morphogenesis. The platform integrates a media-perfused dermal tissue with human epidermal keratinocytes within a microfluidic device and supports rapid epidermal stratification following establishment of an air-liquid interface. High-resolution confocal imaging and single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrate that the StrataChip recapitulates key architectural and molecular features of the human epidermis, including distinct basal, spinous, and granular layers, as defined by canonical differentiation markers and adhesion molecule organization. Single-cell profiling reveals transcriptionally distinct basal and spinous subpopulations, including transitional states associated with suprabasal commitment. Live 3D imaging in situ captures keratinocyte morphodynamics, including basal cell delamination and asymmetric division in early stages of epidermal stratification. Altogether, StrataChip provides a robust platform that is capable of dynamic and mechanistic interrogation of how gene regulation and cellular mechanical changes are coupled during epidermal morphogenesis.

title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
text: Abstract Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

title: Artificial Intelligence in EGFR-mutated NSCLC: Reframing the Therapeutic and Biological Landscape
text: Despite advances in targeted therapy, acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major challenge in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), owing to its biological heterogeneity, temporal evolution, and increasing therapeutic complexity. This narrative review critically examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to integrate clinical, molecular, imaging, and pharmacological data across the osimertinib treatment trajectory, with particular emphasis on resistance monitoring and clinical pharmacology. We discuss natural language processing for clinical data extraction and pharmacovigilance; digital pathology, radiomics, and multimodal learning for molecular pre-screening and risk stratification; longitudinal circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) modelling; and emerging applications of synthetic data, generative simulation, and digital twins. We also explore opportunities to integrate machine learning with pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling, exposure–response analyses, therapeutic drug monitoring, and model-informed precision dosing. Although selected AI approaches have demonstrated promising performance in retrospective studies and external or prospective silent evaluations, their ability to identify specific acquired resistance mechanisms and improve clinical outcomes through model-guided interventions remains unproven. Experience from other solid tumours provides methodological precedents, but disease-specific validation is required. Future progress will depend on multicentre longitudinal datasets integrating drug exposure, molecular evolution, treatment-related toxicity, and clinical outcomes, together with rigorous prospective evaluation. AI may complement established pharmacometric approaches to support more individualized, biologically informed treatment strategies in EGFR-mutated NSCLC.

title: Cloud computing for clinical next-generation sequencing testing
Gene therapy strategy to treat Cornelia de Lange syndrome due to Hdac8 Deficiency
text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a rare, multi-system genetic disorder characterized by developmental and cognitive impairments with systemic manifestations. Among the genes associated with CdLS, loss-of-function variants in HDAC8 account for approximately 4% of cases (referred to as CdLS5), causing the dysregulation of the cohesin complex, a core pathogenic mechanism of the disorder. Currently, no gene-based therapeutic strategy exists to directly address CdLS resulting from HDAC8 deficiency. Here, we created a new CdLS5 mouse model by introducing a clinically reported HDAC8 p.Ile19Ser variant in the mouse Hdac8 gene using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Comprehensive molecular, morphological, and behavioral characterization revealed that the new Hdac8I19S mouse strain exhibits a robust phenotype, including marked alterations in deacetylase activity and pronounced developmental and behavioral deficits. This model was subsequently used to evaluate a gene augmentation approach aimed at increasing HDAC8 protein levels and restoring cohesin function through delivery of human HDAC8 transgene. Two AAV vectors driving expression of human HDAC8 were assessed. Although efficient delivery and robust expression were achieved, only modest effects on Smc3 acetylation, a key HDAC8 substrate, were observed, and no significant improvement in cognitive or behavioral phenotypes was detected. Overall, these findings demonstrate that postnatal HDAC8 gene augmentation resulted in limited biochemical correction and minimal phenotypic improvement under the conditions tested. These results highlight important biological considerations, including target engagement and developmental timing, that should be considered in the development of effective therapies for cohesin-related disorders.

title: Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT): An NCI-CIBMTR genomic medicine initiative in hematopoietic cell transplantation
text: BackgroundGenomic studies in hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) are limited by sample sizes and targeted approaches. MethodsThe Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT) project is a collaboration between the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the CIBMTR(R) designed to investigate recipient and donor determinants of HCT outcomes. We are generating genome-wide SNP-array genotyping for all samples, and sequencing and methylation profiling for selected subsets. We report study design and cohort characteristics and present two proof-of-concept analyses: comparison of conventional and machine learning prediction of overall survival after HCT in 9,262 patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and assessment of inherited susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) among 19,750 HCT donors using polygenic scores (PGS). ResultsGS-BMT includes 30,718 donor-recipient pairs who received allogeneic HCT in the United States between 2000 and 2019. In AML, clinical variables alone provided modest prediction for post-transplant survival, with similar performance for Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and deep neural network survival models (C-index=0.63, 0.62, and 0.62, respectively). In donors, CHIP-PGS did not differ by age (p=0.76) but was modestly lower in unrelated vs. related donors (-0.06 standard deviation [SD]; p=0.002). In an illustrative analysis assuming risk of event increases by 50% or 80% per PGS-SD, the top 5.2% and 12.3% of the donors, respectively, would have at least twice the risk of a donor with the average PGS. ConclusionsGS-BMT establishes a large genomic platform aiming to improve individualized risk prediction, donor selection, and precision medicine in HCT.

title: A precision medicine approach to allergic contact dermatitis: current evidence and future opportunities
text: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a common inflammatory skin disease arising from interactions between environmental exposures and individual susceptibility. While patch testing and allergen avoidance remain cornerstones of management, advances in genetics, barrier biology and digital technologies present opportunities for more precise approaches to prediction, prevention and management. Here, we review evidence for genetic susceptibility and gene–environment interactions in ACD, including variation in epidermal barrier function, immune regulation and xenobiotic metabolism, and consider the role of genetic counselling in interpreting and communicating risk. We further examine emerging applications of artificial intelligence in patch-test interpretation, exposure assessment and predictive modelling. Finally, we propose a future framework for precision approaches to ACD, integrating genomic, phenotypic and exposomic data to characterise individual risk and disease endotypes. These insights could inform more individualised prevention, diagnosis and therapeutic selection, while supporting personalised skincare and safer topical product design. Although substantial challenges remain, convergence of these fields may shift ACD from a predominantly reactive model towards a more predictive, preventive and personalised framework.

title: Pooled Multiplex Amplicon Massive Parallel Sequencing for High-Throughput Confirmation of Whole-Genome Sequencing Potentially Pathogenic Variants in Patients with Parkinsonism
text: Whole-genome sequencing identifies large numbers of genetic variants, although only a subset requires independent confirmation for clinical interpretation. Sanger sequencing remains the standard confirmation method but is impractical for large-scale variant verification. We developed and evaluated a strategy for variant confirmation based on multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing of pooled DNA samples. Whole-genome sequencing data were obtained from 86 individuals, including patients with parkinsonism and controls. Variants were selected using phenotype-driven filtering, ClinVar classification, and pathogenicity assessment criteria. A total of 307 variants were targeted using a custom amplicon panel comprising 290 amplicons. DNA samples were normalized, pooled into 16 mixtures, and sequenced following automated library preparation. Variant presence and sequencing quality were assessed using standard bioinformatic tools. Of the 307 selected variants, 243 were successfully confirmed. Unconfirmed variants included sequencing artifacts (18), insufficiently covered targets (5), large insertions or deletions exceeding 12 base pairs (36), and variants located within homopolymeric regions (5). Results for selected variants were concordant with Sanger sequencing, and observed variant frequencies corresponded to expected frequencies in pooled samples. This approach provides a robust, rapid, and cost-effective method for high-throughput genetic variants confirming identified by whole-genome sequencing while requiring only limited DNA input. Despite complete concordance with Sanger sequencing, larger validation studies are needed before multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing can replace routine confirmatory testing. Key PointsO_LIDesign and application of a high-throughput verification strategy for WGS variants with minimal DNA input requirements C_LIO_LIReliable and independent confirmation of WGS findings C_LIO_LIUtilization of multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing (MPS) in sample mixtures C_LIO_LIDetection of point mutations, small indels and duplications. title: Towards a Wearable Alcohol Biosensor: Examining the Accuracy of BAC Estimates From New-Generation Transdermal Technology Using Large-Scale Human Testing and Machine Learning Algorithms
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] The study will employ a combined laboratory-ambulatory design. Participants will engage in ambulatory assessment over the course of 14 days, wearing biosensors assessing transdermal alcohol concentration (TAC) and providing breathalyzer readings in real-world contexts. Also during this period, participants will attend three laboratory alcohol-administration sessions scheduled at one-week intervals, with alcohol dose and rate of consumption manipulated within and between participants, respectively. Laboratory visits will also double as ambulatory orientation, check-in, and close-out sessions.

title: Attitudes and Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots in the Peer Review of Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine Research: A Large-Scale, International Cross-Sectional Survey
text: BackgroundGenerative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are being explored for their potential to support the peer review process by improving efficiency and analytical capacity. While early applications show promise, concerns regarding ethics, privacy, and research integrity remain, and their use within traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine (TCIM) remains underexplored. This study examines TCIM researchers attitudes and perceptions regarding the use of GenAI chatbots in peer review through a large-scale international survey. MethodsCorresponding authors of TCIM-related publications indexed in Ovid MEDLINE were invited to participate in an online, anonymous, international cross-sectional survey distributed via SurveyMonkey. The questionnaire collected data on demographic characteristics, the perceived importance of GenAI in peer review, the likelihood of adoption, and the perceived benefits and concerns. ResultsA total of 889 eligible respondents participated. Overall, 40.25% (n=285/708) reported a positive perception of GenAI in peer review, and 41.67% (n=295/708) considered it important to the field. 34.24% researchers reported being likely (n=253/739) or 18.27% (135/739) very likely (totaling 52.51%) to use GenAI in peer review, highlighting a gap between perceived importance and intended adoption. Identified benefits included improved efficiency (50.72%, n=350/690), reduced reviewer workload (51.16%, n=353/690), and generation of constructive feedback (46.30%, n=319/689), reflecting respondents selecting "agree." Concerns included bias (49.85%, n=333/668), lack of transparency (42.86%, n=285/665), inaccuracies (49.40%, n=329/666), accountability challenges (45.20%, n=301/666), and data privacy risks (36.05%, n=239/663). Most respondents believed that peer reviewers require either some training (43.91%, n=310/706) or a lot of training (40.93%, n=289/706) to use GenAI chatbots effectively in peer review. ConclusionRespondents reported perceived benefits of GenAI in peer review, alongside notable concerns regarding its use. While opinions were mixed, findings suggest both perceived utility and apprehension about potential risks. Further work is needed to understand these perspectives better and to explore how GenAI can be responsibly integrated into peer-review processes.

title: Real-time neuromorphic audio and vision perception for autonomous robotic applications: Integration and experimental evaluation on a rover platform
text: Neuromorphic sensing and computing offer a promising alternative to conventional deep learning pipelines for mobile robots, where perception must run continuously under tight latency and energy constraints. However, most neuromorphic solutions are still evaluated offline or on isolated benchmarks, and their integration into complete robotic systems remains largely unexplored. In this technical report, a four-wheel rover platform is presented that combines three real-time perception pipelines: a classical audio tagging pipeline based on Pretrained Audio Neural Networks (PANNs) running on an NVIDIA Jetson GPU, a neuromorphic audio pipeline in which a spiking neural network (SNN) is deployed on the SynSense Xylo Audio~2 chip, and a neuromorphic vision pipeline in which events from an event-based camera are processed by the SpikeYOLO spiking detector for traffic cone detection. On the Xylo chip, the whole processing chain---from the microphone signal to the classification of low- and high-pitched sounds---is performed on-chip, while the host only configures the device and reads the output neurons. All models are deployed as containerised services and integrated through ROS~2, and a configurable action dispatcher maps the detected classes to robot behaviours, closing the loop between perception and actuation. The platform is demonstrated in a proof-of-concept scenario in which the robot reacts to sound classes detected by both audio pipelines and detects traffic cones with the event camera, showing the feasibility of integrating neuromorphic hardware into a multimodal robotic platform operating in real time.

title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
text: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.

title: Design and evaluation of probe-capture sequencing for clinical Neisseria gonorrhoeae specimens
text: Characterizing the molecular epidemiology of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is essential for understanding disease burden, elucidating transmission dynamics, and informing clinical decision-making and public health interventions. Given that routine, culture-independent diagnostics rapidly and sensitively detect this difficult-to-cultivate pathogen, aligning genomic surveillance with these workflows is necessary to understand its epidemiology and evolutionary dynamics. To address this challenge, we investigated the utility of probe-capture sequencing to selectively enrich for pathogen-specific DNA during next-generation sequencing. Custom biotinylated oligonucleotide baits were designed using genetic information from publicly available genomes hosted on Pathogenwatch. Of the 32,574 assemblies, 2,877 representative genomes were selected to inform probe generation using core genome amino acid distance clustering and representation of unique resistance-associated genotypes and predicted resistance phenotypes. The resulting probe set provided generous coverage of the reference genome, N. gonorrhoeae FA 1090, with 94.6% nucleotide coverage and 99.3% of annotated genes covered by at least one probe. Piloting this technology on 12 clinical urine specimens with variable relative pathogen abundances revealed that probe-capture sequencing substantially increased the relative abundance of N. gonorrhoeae sequence reads from a complex sample (fold-change range, 226 - 2046), enabling considerable genome coverage, the construction of high-quality genome assemblies, and the detection of resistance-associated genotypes. These findings demonstrate that probe-capture sequencing is a viable method for enriching N. gonorrhoeae genetic material from clinical samples, enabling culture-independent genomic investigations into the epidemiology of hard-to-culture pathogens and providing actionable insights to inform clinical and public health interventions. IMPORTANCEUnderstanding the molecular epidemiology of bacterial pathogens can illuminate population diversity, transmission dynamics, and genotypes associated with bacterial traits and clinical outcomes. Difficulties in cultivation hinder our ability to understand the epidemiology of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Aligning genomic surveillance methodologies with existing clinical diagnostic modalities is essential to guiding the implementation of innovative genomic surveillance. In this paper, we used representative public genome assemblies to design custom biotinylated oligonucleotide baits to successfully increase pathogen-specific DNA yield from complex clinical urine specimens during next-generation sequencing. Probe-capture sequencing markedly improved detection of pathogen-specific genetic material from clinical specimens, enabling construction of high-quality genome assemblies and detection of resistance-associated genotypes. Collectively, we demonstrate that probe-capture sequencing is a viable method for sequencing hard-to-culture pathogens from clinical specimens, highlighting how this technology could strengthen genomic investigations into the epidemiology of these pathogens and provide actionable insights to inform clinical decision-making and public health interventions.

title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA
text: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.

title: Detection Technology of Peripheral Blood ctDNA Based on CRISPR/Cas and Gold Nanoparticles
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study tests a new, fast blood test that may help detect very small traces of tumor DNA in the bloodstream. When tumor cells die, they release small pieces of DNA called circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) into the blood. Finding these pieces can help doctors diagnose cancer, monitor how well treatment is working, and detect cancer recurrence earlier. However, ctDNA is present in very small amounts and is hard to detect with current methods. Newer techniques such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) can find ctDNA, but they are expensive, require specialized laboratories, and take days to return results. This study evaluates a new testing method called "CRISPR/Cas12a combined with gold nanoparticle detection." This method uses a gene-editing protein (Cas12a) that can recognize a specific mutation in the BRCA1 gene and a gold nanoparticle-based readout that shows results within about 30 minutes, using portable equipment. The main purpose of this study is to find out how accurate, sensitive, and specific this new test is compared with NGS, which is considered the gold standard. The study will also check whether the portable device works consistently across different hospitals and whether the test results match patients' responses to treatment. The study will enroll adult cancer patients treated at participating hospitals and a group of healthy volunteers. All participants will provide about 3 mL of blood (less than one teaspoon). No additional invasive procedures or extra hospital visits are required beyond routine blood draws. For cancer patients, part of the blood sample will be tested with the new method and part will be tested with standard NGS, and the two results will be compared. Healthy volunteers' blood will be used to confirm that the test does not produce false positive results. There is no direct physical harm from the test itself, since it is performed on blood samples in the laboratory. Participants will receive the ctDNA test free of charge, and their test results may help their doctors better understand their disease. The results of this study may help develop a rapid, low-cost, bedside test for tumor DNA, which could improve cancer diagnosis and monitoring in the future.

title: Combining Gene Editing and iPS to Study and Treat Monogenic Autoinflammatory Diseases
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Type I interferonopathies (T1I) are rare autoinflammatory diseases characterized by dysregulated type I interferon signaling, leading to severe multisystem inflammation, including skin and lung involvement. STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) is an autosomal dominant T1I associated with severe systemic inflammation, skin ulcers, and progressive interstitial lung disease. Current treatments are often insufficient, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies. This project aims to develop patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, combined with somatic cell differentiation and 3D organoid technologies, to investigate SAVI pathogenesis and assess the feasibility and efficacy of gene editing (GE). By enabling precise correction of disease-causing mutations, GE may overcome the limitations of conventional gene replacement approaches and provide a proof of concept for future targeted therapies.

title: Gene Editing For Sickle Cell Disease
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: RECRUITING] This study is being done to test the safety of a new treatment called gene editing in Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) patients and to see if a single dose of this genetically modified cellular product will increase the amount of a certain hemoglobin called fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and help reduce the symptoms of SCD. Primary Objective * To assess the safety of autologous infusion of clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/ CRISPR associated protein (Cas9)-edited CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in patients with severe SCD. Secondary Objective * To assess the efficacy autologous infusion of CRISPR/Cas9 genome-edited CD34+ HSPCs into patients with severe SCD.

title: Automation of Gamete Preparation, Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI), Embryo Culture, and Vitrification
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: COMPLETED] Patients suffering from infertility may seek assisted conception treatment. In a full treatment cycle, the sperm and eggs (gametes) from the intended parents will be looked after by skilled laboratory staff (embryologists) who will rely on manual laboratory processes to achieve fertilization. The most commonly employed method to achieve fertilization is intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), a treatment that involves the injection of a single sperm cell directly inside an egg. The embryos so obtained are then be maintained in an appropriate environment (incubator) for several days before deciding whether they can be immediately used to attempt to establish a pregnancy (embryo transfer), or should be frozen in preparation for a future treatment (cryopreservation). The laboratory steps required to complete a full assisted conception treatment (from sperm and egg retrieval, to fertilization, and then to embryo transfer and/or cryopreservation) are often manual and time-consuming, and thus the success of the treatment is highly dependent on the skill of individual staff and outcomes can be affected by fatigue, stress, and workload. The combination of robotics and artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to provide improvements to, and standardize, the fertility laboratory, but such integration has not been achieved routinely. Other medical fields, such as regenerative medicine, have long benefited from the implementation of robotic solutions; however, modern automation has yet to find its way into the fertility laboratory. The goal for Conceivable Life Sciences (the study sponsor) is the delivery of a suite of solutions that, collectively, will allow a fully autonomous ICSI cycle to take place (from sperm/egg preparation, to sperm injection, to embryo culture and cryopreservation) in an effort to reduce costs, assist laboratory staff, and possibly, improve outcomes. The purpose of this study is to deliver a core aspect of this project: the digital control and individual automation of all key steps of a complete laboratory workflow. The data generated in this study will help the future development of these automated systems. Patients undergoing an ICSI treatment may be recruited in this study. Their gametes (sperm and/or eggs) may be distributed across two groups (test and control) and undergo one or more elements of an automated full assisted conception workflow (for the test group) or a standard assisted conception workflow (for the control group). Robotic automation may include any of the following steps: robotic sperm preparation, robotic oocyte selection and denudation, robotic sperm injection, automated embryo culture, and automated cryopreservation. The resulting embryos may be employed for embryo transfer. The main hypothesis of this study is that the use of robotic assistants as part of a full assisted conception cycle may improve laboratory workflows without reducing the treatment success rates.

title: Proof of Concept of the Aiinane Preoperative Risk Assessment Tool.
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] BACKGROUND: Each year, over 13,000 patients in Catalonia and more than 4 million worldwide experience last-minute surgery cancellations (LMC) due to preoperative inefficiencies. As anaesthesia services struggle to meet surgical demands, thorough preoperative evaluations become challenging. Current resource-intensive pre-anaesthetic assessments are undermined by high demand, causing inefficiency. However, proper assessment identifies that most patients (\>70%) are low-risk and ensures high-risk patients are adequately prepared by analyzing risk profiles, health status, medical history, treatment, and lab results. RATIONALE: Previous attempts to improve preoperative risk assessment have mainly relied on self-administered questionnaires to detect at-risk patients. The investigators have identified a care model that enhances quality by adding value to preoperative risk assessment. By combining anaesthesiology expertise with AI techniques, the investigators developed an automated digital environment to detect risks, optimize visits, avoid cancellations, and reduce postoperative complications. This system uses parameterized medical knowledge to verify responses and objectively assess patient risk by integrating multiple data sources. The investigators have developed a Class IIa active diagnostic and monitoring product, a Medical Device Software (MDSW, EMDN V92), to support clinical decision-making in an automated digital preoperative environment. It helps assess patients and flags low-risk from medium/high-risk individuals, reporting personalized needs to the medical team. The software was developed exclusively by independent researchers from Bellvitge University Hospital and the Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL). HYPOTHESIS: The tool has been tested successfully on fictitious patients in controlled preclinical scenarios. The aim now is a proof-of-concept study to verify its performance with real patients in uncontrolled, real-world settings. This is a Clinical Performance Research Study, aligned with MDSW Clinical Evaluation Guidelines (MDR, MDCG 2020-1) for (EU) 2017/745, and authorized by the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS) and the local Ethics Committee. MAIN OBJECTIVE: The clinical trial aims to verify that the software (aiinane), supporting preanesthetic assessment and preoperative risk estimation, is fit for its intended purpose and performs as expected under normal conditions of use. This is an observational, non-interventional, single-center, prospective, longitudinal adult cohort study. The target population is any adult (\>18 years) of any gender undergoing breast cancer surgery.

title: Virtual Human Twins as Tools for Personalized Clinical Care in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: a Pilot Study
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Heart failure (HF) is a heterogeneous clinical syndrome characterized by substantial inter-individual variability in pathophysiology and response to treatment. Precision medicine approaches are therefore needed to better account for this heterogeneity and tailor therapeutic strategies to individual patients. Virtual human twins represent one such approach, integrating multimodal clinical, biological, imaging, physiological, and omics data into patient-specific computational models to model disease mechanisms and predict individual therapeutic response. VITAL-HF is a prospective cohort pilot study designed to clinically evaluate the ability of the VITAL cardiovascular virtual human twin to predict individual response to spironolactone in patients with HF. Adult patients with HF with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) \> 40% who have a clinical indication for spironolactone as part of routine care will be enrolled and followed for 3 months. The primary objective is to assess the ability of the VITAL cardiovascular virtual human twin to discriminate responders from non-responders to spironolactone. Response is defined as a ≥20% reduction in NT-proBNP levels 3 months after spironolactone initiation. Virtual twin predictions will be generated for research purposes only and will not influence treatment decisions or patient management.

title: Virtual Twins as Tools for Personalized Clinical Care in Renal Denervation - Pilot Study
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] High blood pressure (hypertension) is a common condition. Despite the availability of several medications, many patients continue to have poorly controlled blood pressure. Renal denervation (RDN), a minimally invasive procedure that reduces overactive kidney nerves, has emerged as a potential treatment for certain patients with difficult-to-control hypertension. However, not all patients benefit from this procedure, and there is currently no reliable way to predict who will respond. The VITAL-RDN study (Virtual twins as tools for personalized clinical care in renal denervation - Pilot study) aims to test whether a "digital twin" can help predict which patients are most likely to respond to renal denervation. A digital twin is a personalized computer model built from an individual patient's clinical, biological, and physiological data. It is designed to simulate how that patient's cardiovascular system functions and how it may respond to treatment. The main objective of this pilot study is to evaluate whether the digital twin can accurately distinguish between patients who will respond to renal denervation and those who will not. A responder is defined as a patient whose daytime systolic blood pressure decreases by at least 5 mmHg three months after the RDN. Three groups of patients will be enrolled: 30 patients with resistant hypertension or other clinical indications for renal denervation. 20 patients with untreated primary hypertension who are starting blood pressure-lowering medication. 10 patients with primary aldosteronism who are scheduled for surgical adrenalectomy. In addition to evaluating prediction of response to renal denervation, the study will also assess the performance of the digital twin in predicting response to antihypertensive medication or adrenalectomy in the respective subgroups. If successful, this approach could support more personalized treatment decisions, reduce unnecessary procedures, and improve blood pressure control by matching the right therapy to the right patient.

title: Real-World Data Linkage Research Platform
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This study aims to address the lack of intelligent governance tools in clinical data management to promote efficient governance and secure sharing of real-world health data. To achieve this, a self-adaptive, automated governance intelligent agent will be developed based on a High-Order Programming (HOP) architecture, integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and deep learning techniques. The agent will continuously monitor and correct data quality issues in real time, improving data accuracy and usability. In parallel, the project will establish a trusted data-sharing framework by integrating AI Confidential Computing (AICC) with Trusted Data Matrix (TDM) technologies. This framework will enable secure, real-time cross-institutional data exchange and collaborative computation while protecting sensitive information. Overall, the study aims to transform fragmented clinical data into high-quality, standardized, and securely accessible resources, thereby facilitating the circulation of data value and advancing collaborative medical research.

title: AI-driven Personalized Exercise Feedback Program on Exercise Adherence in Traumatic Brain Injury
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] This study aims to develop and evaluate an AI-driven Personalized Exercise Feedback Program (AI-PEF) to enhance exercise adherence and health outcomes in mTBI patients. Methods: AI-PEF integrates the transtheoretical model and self-determination theory with machine learning algorithms to provide real-time, personalized feedback. A phased randomized controlled trial will be conducted: Phase I evaluates feasibility and acceptability through Delphi methods with expert consensus and patient feedback; Phase II validates preliminary outcomes with 30 participants in a 2-arm randomized trial; and Phase III assesses the program's impact on exercise motivation, exercise adherence, functional exercise capacity, post-concussion symptoms, depressive symptoms, sleep quality, physical activity, quality of life, cognitive function, prefrontal cerebral blood flow, cardiac metabolic performance, physiological monitoring, and mHealth app usability with 90 participants in a 3-arm randomized trial. In Phase III, quantitative and qualitative data will be collected in parallel, with qualitative data collected through semi-structured interviews to explore participants' experiences and perceptions of the intervention.

title: Global partnership to make available 120 million affordable, quality COVID-19 rapid tests for low- and middle-income countries
text: A full access package includes WHO policy guidance on the use of antigen-based rapid diagnostic tests, manufacturer volume guarantees for low and middle-income countries,  catalytic funding to assist governments to deploy the tests and an initial US$50 million procurement fund Several rapid, point-of-care antigen tests are being assessed by WHO for Emergency Use Listing (EUL) Agreements between the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and test manufacturers Abbott and SD Biosensor make available innovative tests priced at a maximum of US$5 for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) The Global Fund commits an initial US$50 million to enable countries to purchase the new tests, with the first orders expected to be placed this week Expedited market introduction of these tests in multiple LMICs is being supported through the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Unitaid, FIND, CHAI, and their partners This is the latest move from the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator to develop, procure and distribute critical new tools to fight the pandemic; new tests are urgently needed to meet the huge unmet needs for testing worldwide   A set of agreements to make available, for low and middle-income countries, affordable, high-quality COVID-19 antigen rapid tests were today announced by the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator. Organizations involved in the milestone agreement include the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI), the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND), the Global Fund, Unitaid, and the World Health Organization (WHO). As part of this comprehensive, end-to-end effort, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has executed separate volume guarantee agreements with rapid diagnostic test (RDT) producers Abbott and SD Biosensor. These two arrangements will make available to LMICs 120 million antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag RDTs) – priced at a maximum of US$5 per unit – over a period of six months. These tests provide results in 15–30 minutes, rather than hours or days, and will enable expansion of testing, particularly in countries that do not have extensive laboratory facilities or trained health workers to implement molecular (polymerase-chain reaction or PCR) tests. The tests developed by Abbott and SD Biosensor are highly portable, reliable, and easy to administer, making testing possible in near-person, decentralized healthcare settings. Both companies’ tests are faster and cheaper than laboratory-based tests, enabling countries to increase the pace of testing, tracing and treating people for COVID-19 at the point of care particularly in areas with under-resourced health systems. A number of other Ag RDTs are at various stages of development and assessment. To scale up the Ag RDTs, the Global Fund today announced that it has made available an initial US$50 million from its COVID-19 Response Mechanism to enable countries to purchase at least 10 million of the new rapid tests for LMICs at the guaranteed price, with the first orders expected to be placed this week through the Global Fund’s pooled procurement mechanism. FIND and WHO are working together to accelerate appropriate use by supporting implementation research that will optimize Ag RDT use in multiple LMICs, in line with WHO guidance. This includes provision of catalytic volumes of tests to understand how Ag RDTs can best fit into health systems. Unitaid and Africa CDC will combine resources to initiate the roll out of these tests in up to 20 countries in Africa starting in October 2020. This multi-million-dollar intervention, currently undergoing final sign-off by their Boards, is designed to engage multiple partners active in the COVID-19 response in these countries, such as CHAI, African Society for Laboratory Medicine (ASLM) and local organizations. title: Development of a deep learning model for glomerulus detection and segmentation in kidney histopathology images
text: BackgroundEstimation of nephron number, an indicator of renal reserve, requires quantitative assessment of glomerular number and size in kidney biopsy specimens. We aimed to develop an automated system for quantitative measurement of glomerular areas from clinical kidney biopsy images, across diverse kidney diseases. MethodsWe developed a two-stage deep learning system combining Faster R-CNN for glomerular detection in whole-slide images (WSIs) and DeepLabV3+ for segmentation. Of 114 kidney biopsies (228 WSIs), 104 were used for model development and 10 for independent final evaluation. Agreement was assessed using the F1-score for detection, the Dice coefficient for segmentation, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for glomerular area measurement. Analysis was performed at 40x total magnification (2.331 m/pixel) and validated against 400x images. ResultsIn the independent evaluation set, the artificial intelligence (AI) model achieved a mean F1-score of 0.851 for detection, compared with 0.888 among experts. For segmentation, the Dice coefficient was 0.959 {+/-} 0.011 and the per-pair ICC (2,1) for area measurement was 0.989 {+/-} 0.009; both were comparable to inter-expert agreement. Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -344 m{superscript 2} (95% limits of agreement, -1904 to 1216 m{superscript 2}) between 40x and 400x measurements. ConclusionThe two-stage model achieved glomerular segmentation and area measurement comparable to expert agreement in independent clinical data, with detection performance approaching inter-expert agreement, and provided reliable measurements at low magnification. This automated approach may facilitate large-scale quantitative kidney pathology and nephron number estimation from clinical kidney biopsies.

title: Applications of Fairness Training in Artificial Intelligence to Ophthalmic Disease Diagnosis using External Eye Photographs
text: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85{middle dot}4%, comparable to ViT 82{middle dot}6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86{middle dot}3%; LLaVA 84{middle dot}8%; ViT 84{middle dot}7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86{middle dot}3% and 85{middle dot}9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
text: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analyzed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

title: Insulin resistance reverses despite weight gain with pan-PPAR agonism, revealing its plasma molecular correlates in type 2 diabetes
text: Insulin resistance (IR) and body weight are closely linked in type 2 diabetes (T2D), so their molecular correlates are hard to separate in observational data. Pan-PPAR agonism offers a test, because it improves insulin sensitivity while body weight increases. In the ChiHOPE cohort of 835 T2D patients from two randomized phase 3 trials of chiglitazar, 53% of chiglitazar-treated patients with HOMA-IR-defined IR at baseline no longer met the IR threshold after treatment, compared with 29% with placebo and 32% with sitagliptin, while BMI rose. We integrated plasma metabolomics and proteomics into a molecular estimate of HOMA-IR. It outperformed routine clinical measures, disagreed with HOMA-IR classification in 27% of patients, and identified adverse lipid, liver and inflammatory profiles within each HOMA-IR class. With chiglitazar, the molecular estimate fell despite weight gain, with lower proteoglycan 4 and higher glutamine and glycine. Circulating markers of IR can therefore improve without weight loss. title: Global Adoption of openEHR Clinical Data Repositories: A Vendor and Community Survey
text: The openEHR standard provides an open, vendor-neutral architecture for clinical data repositories (CDRs), yet its real-world deployment has not been systematically documented. We conducted a dual-perspective survey combining a vendor survey of openEHR CDR providers with a community survey of openEHR practitioners. Eleven vendor organisations reported deployments across 21 countries and over 100 institutions and health regions. A complementary community survey (n=29, 17 countries) provided context on regulatory environments, adoption drivers, and barriers. Combined, the surveys cover 28 countries, 25 of them with a reported openEHR CDR deployment. Three findings emerge: openEHR has achieved national-scale presence through two distinct channels. Through vendor-market convergence, openEHR-based systems cover the majority of regional health authorities without a national mandate, including 19 of 21 Swedish regions, 3 of 4 Norwegian health regions, and 16 of 21 Finnish wellbeing services counties. Through national health record adoption, governments have built or procured national systems on openEHR as their technical foundation, including Ireland, Malta, Greece, Slovenia, and, by community report, Iran. Across Europe, this constitutes an openEHR-based interoperability infrastructure already in place across multiple EU member states. We identified no country in which openEHR is named in binding national regulation, creating structural fragility and an unrealised opportunity for alignment with the European Health Data Space (EHDS). Second, 61% of deployments serve primary use only, and 12% support both primary and secondary use. Third, lack of openEHR-specific knowledge is the most consistent adoption barrier across all geographies and deployment tiers. Adoption is driven by practitioner need and innovation, not by regulatory mandate.

title: Deep learning-based electrocardiographic differentiation of Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior myocardial infarction: explainability, human-AI interaction, and a utilization bias hypothesis
text: Background and AimsArtificial intelligence (AI) may help differentiate Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) on electrocardiograms (ECGs). We developed an ECG image-based model and evaluated whether AI assistance and visual explanations improved reader performance, overall and by reader background. MethodsA self-supervised three-architecture deep learning ensemble was developed and externally validated using 12-lead ECG images from two institutions, recorded [≤]14 days after onset regardless of reperfusion. A four-phase reader study compared unaided interpretation, a reference sheet, and AI assistance (Phases 1-3). In Phase 4, readers were randomized to the reference sheet alone, AI predictions, or predictions with gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Correctness was analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models. ResultsCohorts comprised 832 development and 95 external validation participants. External validation accuracy was 0.914, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.970 (95% CI, 0.938-0.992), or 0.958 using first recorded ECGs. Among 70 readers, the estimated probability of correct diagnosis increased from 0.632 unaided to 0.864 with AI (odds ratio [OR], 3.71; P<0.001). In Phase 4, AI assistance improved accuracy vs reference sheet (OR, 4.28; 95% CI, 3.08-5.95), and Grad-CAM added value (OR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.04-2.25). In exploratory analyses, less experienced readers gained more; with AI, non-cardiologists outperformed cardiologists. Mean AI-assisted reader accuracy remained below model accuracy. ConclusionsAn ECG image-based ensemble differentiated Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI and improved reader performance, particularly with visual explanations. Experience-related differences emphasize the need for effective human-AI interaction.
